newsitem.title: ROMANIA: Romania PM defends government in confidence debate.
newsitem.headline: Romania PM defends government in confidence debate.

text.p: Romanian Prime Minister Victor Ciorbea told his country on Friday it had no choice but to back proposed fast-track market reforms, and he looked almost certain to win the support of the centrist-dominated parliament.

The leftist opposition, ejected from office last November after seven years in power, acknowledged that Ciorbea's programme had widespread support but warned that austerity measures had pushed the country close to breaking point.

Ciorbea said prolonged mismanagement by the ex-communists who took over following the 1989 execution of dictator Nicolae Ceausescu had pitched the country into crisis. His government was now taming inflation, stabilising the leu currency and preparing Romania for integration with the European Union.
"The current situation is the legacy of the former government," he told a joint session of parliament.

"Industrial policy in recent years was a failure. We will support only those sectors which can compete with our future EU partners. It is not the government which is closing down factories. They are being closed down by market laws."

Members were almost certain later in the day to defeat one of two opposition confidence motions accusing ministers of failing to keep election promises to improve living standards, cut taxes and help industry and agriculture.
President Emil Constantinescu and his government have pledged to press ahead with reforms which have cut average monthly salaries in recent months to the equivalent of less than $80.
International lenders have praised their efforts, with the International Monetary Fund extending credits of $430 million and the World Bank offering a further $550 million in loans.

Opinion polls show most Romanians support reforms despite a widening gap in living standards with other ex-communist countries like Poland, Hungary and the Czech Republic. Trade unions have mounted only minor protests so far.

Mircea Cosea, reform minister in the ousted leftist administration, acknowledged that Ciorbea's government had won international confidence with a "classic economic model". But he urged the government not to squander its opportunities.
"For the first time we have layoffs in the private sector, which has come under pressure from tax policies," he said.

"You enjoy great popular support and foreign support, you have a market infrastructure set up by the former government. Don't miss the opportunities to develop Romania. These opportunities are on the brink of being lost."

Many commentators have said the opposition motion amounts to little more than an attempt to divert attention from its own serious divisions. The main opposition Party of Social Democracy (PDSR), headed by former president Ion Iliescu, is riven by a revolt by a faction demanding leadership changes.
Cosea said the government had sunk into a pattern of "taking steps only when pressed by the IMF and World Bank".
In the past week, with some World Bank credits up for discussion and an IMF monitoring team in Bucharest, the government has moved to approve measures demanded by Western lenders and investors.

Ministers approved rules this week for capital gains repatriation long demanded for improving on disappointing capital inflows. It also announced measures to dismantle large government utilities and pledged to cut profit and wage taxes.
